catalog_quote: Rumsen stress appears to fall predominantly on the first syllable of a word as in Mutsun (Okrand 1977). In regards to Mutsun, Okrand states that “the best evidence for word-initial stress comes from non-native vocabulary. If a loanword from Spanish has stress on a syllable other than that which is stressed in Spanish, the shift must be due to Mutsun stress patterns” (ibid.: 98). The same also seems to hold true for Rumsen, which also has Spanish loan words with the stress shifted to first syllable: púyyito ‘chicken’ from pollito; káwwayo ‘horse’ from caballo; and kásteyano ‘Spanish’ from castellano (Harrington 1981), the original Spanish words being stressed on the penultimate syllable.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (7 pp., letter, text layer present, Producer Mac OS X Quartz, created 2010-01-20; running header "Kansas Working Papers in Linguistics, Vol. 31, 39-45") and re-extracted page 2 (= p. 40) with extracted text independently of the. Section "3. Stress" is on p. 40 and the entire quoted passage from "Rumsen stress appears to fall predominantly on the first syllable of a word as in Mutsun (Okrand 1977)" through "the original Spanish words being stressed on the penultimate syllable" is there verbatim, including the three loans púyyito, káwwayo, kásteyano and the Okrand p. 98 quotation. The saved KWPL landing page carries citation_date 2009, volume 31, pp. 39-45, DOI 10.17161/KWPL.1808.5719,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word; the evidence offered is Spanish loanwords (recorded by Harrington from Isabel Meadows) whose penultimate Spanish stress has shifted to the initial syllable, paralleling Okrand's word-initial stress analysis for the closely related Mutsun.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the author hedges ('appears to fall predominantly'), and the claim rests on three loanwords plus the Mutsun parallel. Vowel length (written doubled) is phonemic and independent of stress per section 2.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (stress 'of a word'), based on Harrington's transcriptions of narrative text and lexical items; no phrase-level or citation-form discussion. Confidence medium because the source is a short working paper that explicitly calls itself a 'brief preliminary analysis' and no fuller Rumsen phonology (Broadbent 1957, Okrand 1980, Callaghan 1992/2014) could be opened to confirm.
new_statements.identity_note: Rumsen = Rumsien = Carmeleño (Glottolog rums1243, no ISO code; Ethnologue lumps it under Southern Ohlone css). Kaufman 2009's data are Harrington's 1930s notes from Isabel Meadows (Carmel/Monterey); Kroeber 1904's 'Rumsien' is the same Monterey variety. The earlier scan's 'Okrand 1977 Rumsen Grammar' is actually Okrand's Mutsun Grammar (muts1243), a different Costanoan language.
